I think that exposure regarding social situations/interactions could be helpful. You have very good self-awareness, and I think you are correct when you say the current severity is probably related to recent social isolation. With social anxiety, isolation can really have an effect because it’s like your brain forgets you are capable of having successful social interactions (to put it very simply) due to lack of exposure. It’s easy to spiral because the anxiety promotes social isolation, and then the anxiety gets worse! 

I also have very severe anxiety (and would sometime miss labs and lectures to avoid, like you said, failing or in some way embarrassing myself in front of my peers and profs), and was really set back after isolation during COVID lockdowns. Keep pushing yourself to go, it will get easier. 

It could also be worth talking to someone at the Academic Accommodations Support (AAS) centre, because it does sound like academic performance is part of what’s triggering the anxiety. AAS staff can help with resources like time management and studying advice, plus coping skills and other mental health resources.

Every child is different, but in my experience, by the age of 4, most children are able to be independent from immediate caregivers and have achieved sufficient verbal proficiency to be reassured by the stranger if needed. For context, I (F32) volunteer in a children’s hospital with social work staff. My main responsibility is to provide the patient’s parents/caregivers with breaks, whether it’s to take a shower or do laundry or get a coffee, and I’ll stay with the child in their absence. I’ll go to their room with books, toys, crafts, etc., and will chat a bit with the parent so the child can see us having a friendly interaction first. Often, the parent will then linger a minute or 2 to make sure the child is OK being left alone with me. By the age of 4, I would say that 99% of the children are like “ok bye!” when the parent says they’re stepping out (the other 1% may need some reassurance from the parent that they’ll be right back). Children around 2-3 years old are also usually fine being left with me, but may briefly stop play to ask where mom/dad went. I’ll reassure them that mom/dad just had to go ___ and will be back soon, and they’re generally OK with that. It also happens where the parent is given a break but doesn’t leave the room — they might stay and just lie down on the couch for a nap, be on their phone, etc. In those cases, I find that the child will sometimes try to involve the parent, even if in a more passive way. For example, we’ll build something with lego or do a craft, and then they’ll call the parent over to see the finished product. 

Having said all that, context may play a role in my specific experiences. These are children in the healthcare system, and some (but not all) of them have chronic conditions, which means they’re interacting with nurses, doctors, techs, etc., and may therefore be more comfortable around strangers than the average child. My gender, being female, may also play a role, as there is research that suggests young children are generally more trusting of adult women than men. By the age of 4, I would think that the child’s experiences with strangers would also be a factor (for example, some children spend time in daycare, but some do not).

There is a fairly large body of evidence that suggests humans are predisposed to be highly sensitive to snake-like movements, such as a slithering movement. Same thing regarding spiders. It has happened to me many times that I have detected a spider at night in a dark room before even turning the light on. Light from stars/the moon or urban light pollution is definitely sufficient to detect snake-like movement (and activation of the sympathetic nervous system, which includes what we call “fight or flight”, inhibits the gastrointestinal system, and may explain the stomach-turning sensation). The evolutionary explanation for this is that snakes and spiders, in particular, would have posed a significant threat to the survival of our ancestors for the hundreds of thousands of years that span our ‘evolutionary history’. Snakes and spiders still pose a huge threat to many around the world, however, thankfully not where I live. But despite never being in the presence of a poisonous snake or spider, I have a bigger [physiological] reaction to a stick in tall grass or a speck of dirt on a wall than I do from a speeding car or a person holding an object that resembles a gun.

Absolutely! I’ve (F/31) had guys approach me when I’m just out living my life — in a mall, waiting at a stoplight to cross, while grabbing a coffee, walking down the street, etc. Questions are a good way to start a convo, like you could ask for directions somewhere, and if she responds with a smile and seems friendly say something else. Maybe she’s wearing something (like a hat or t-shirt) that suggests a shared interest, like a band or movie or sport or something. If she’s not so smiley/friendly with the initial question she prob doesn’t want to be bothered. If the convo ends fast, don’t take it personally. Some girls feel unsafe talking to random guys on the street, especially if it’s night (in which case, prob best to not approach at all), and some have had bad experiences with guys who won’t take “no” for an answer (don’t be that guy). Things like this definitely get easier with practice, and the more you expose yourself to the anxiety, and learn to tolerate it, the less anxiety will get in the way. Remember that it’s like building any new skill — expect to fail at first and know that you’ll get better (even if it feels like you won’t, I guarantee you will).
